title: Keep a new work skill from fading: spaced retrieval practice
performance: After watching, the viewer closes the material after training, tries the task from memory, checks what they missed, and repeats that short attempt on later days tied to real work, then picks the better plan in a fresh situation.

audience.assumed_prior: Knows their own daily work and has sat through workplace training. Has not met spaced retrieval practice as an idea.
audience.why: Corporate employees; a practitioner posture means short worked example, decisions sooner, density trusted.
audience.motivation: Wants to use a new tool or skill at work without extra effort, and without redoing the training.
audience.context: Watching alone at a desk, between tasks, with a real recent or upcoming training in mind.

strategy.name: scenario_led
strategy.rationale: One recognisable stuck situation (a colleague trained on new software who struggles a week later) carries every idea and returns resolved at the end. The brief asks for one running situation.
strategy.signature_move: Show Sam stuck, name what faded, let Sam try closed-book, reveal the gap, spread the try across days, then return to the original stuck task.

misconceptions.belief: If I re-watch or re-read the training until it feels familiar and easy, I know it.
misconceptions.why_tempting: Familiarity feels like knowing (F7); re-watching is easy and feels productive.

misconceptions.belief: One focused block of practice is the best way to make it stick.
misconceptions.why_tempting: Cramming feels productive and does help for a test soon after (F4).

misconceptions.belief: If my recall attempt is shaky or I get answers wrong, it is not working.
misconceptions.why_tempting: Effort and misses feel like failure; effortless feels like progress.

hook.sketch: Imagine Sam, who spent a full day on new software training. A week later, Sam opens it and cannot remember where to start. (On screen: A week later.)

arc.promise: By the end you will know what Sam could have done in ten minutes, spread over a few days, so the training is still there when the real task arrives, and you can do the same for your own next training.
arc.bridge_from_prior: You have sat through training and found it half gone when the real task showed up. Same thing happened to Sam, so the next step is to see what actually happens to the learning.

sections.goal: the viewer can state that newly learned material fades when not revisited, and fastest soon after learning
sections.recap_after: One line: fading is fastest early, with no figures. Sam's skill is going and nothing is bringing it back.
sections.visual_change: A skill icon on Sam's desk visibly fades steeply on day one then more slowly through the week.

sections.goal: the viewer can explain why practice spread over several days usually lasts longer than the same practice in one block
sections.recap_after: Same effort, two timelines: one block today versus short visits on later days. The spread one usually lasts. Cramming helps for a test tomorrow, not for lasting.
sections.visual_change: Two timelines for the same total effort; the single-block one fades faster after the block while the spread one is lifted at each visit.

sections.goal: the viewer can explain why trying to recall from memory usually beats re-watching, even when it feels harder
sections.recap_after: Re-watching feels familiar and that is not the same as knowing. Closed-book try, then check, helps most. Somewhat hard and some misses is the working zone.
sections.visual_change: Sam re-watches and says it all looks familiar, then closes the screen and cannot start; the gap list on the notepad fills in as Sam checks the answers.

sections.goal: the viewer can carry out a closed-book recall attempt, check the misses, and schedule a repeat on a later day tied to real work
sections.recap_after: Three steps Sam uses on the original task: close it and try, check the misses, repeat on a later day using the tool on a real task.
sections.visual_change: The blank task from the hook is redone step by step; the missed steps shrink on the gap list across two later days.

sections.goal: the viewer can spot a task in their own coming week that can carry a later recall attempt, and tell it apart from re-reading
sections.recap_after: Pick the real task, pick the later day, try from memory first. If you are only looking at it again, it is a re-read.
sections.visual_change: A blank week calendar gets one real task marked and a short recall try placed a few days after training.

arc.payoff: Back to Sam at the same desk, a week on: Sam opens the software, starts the task, misses one step, checks it and carries on. Carry-out line: Close it, try it, check it, and come back another day.

practice_ladder.what: Sam works the three steps on the original situation while the viewer watches.
Quiz in a fresh variation: the viewer chooses the plan, then the answer card explains why.
The viewer picks a real task and a later day in their own week.

recall_moments.question: Say Sam has just finished a short training on a new approval tool. Which plan is most likely to still work weeks later?
options: Re-watch the recording tonight until it feels easy
Tomorrow, close it and try the task from memory, check what was missed, and repeat on a later day
Do all the practice in one long block today
recall_moments.answer: Tomorrow, close it and try the task from memory, check what was missed, and repeat on a later day
recall_moments.tempting_wrong: Re-watch the recording tonight until it feels easy, because feeling familiar seems like knowing it
recall_moments.why: Re-watching feels easy, and that feeling is mistaken for knowing; recall followed by a check, spread over days, usually lasts.

recall_moments.prompt: Spoken callback to Sam's fading skill icon: remember where it dropped fastest? Those early days are when a visit helps most.
Spoken callback to the quiz: that closed-book try is exactly what the better plan did.

transfer_tasks: Pick one tool or skill from your most recent training, choose a real task a few days from now that uses it, and try it from memory first, then check what you missed.

gagne.attention: arc.hook (Sam blank a week after training)
gagne.recall_prior: arc.bridge_from_prior and audience.assumed_prior (own experience of half-lost training)
gagne.guidance: strategy.signature_move and the worked step in sec4_the_step
gagne.practice: recall_moments quiz after sec3, practice_ladder rungs, sec5_own_week

merrill.problem_centred: Sam's stuck situation runs through every section
merrill.demonstration: sec3 and sec4 show Sam doing it
merrill.integration: transfer_tasks and sec5_own_week tie to the viewer's own calendar

mayer.coherence: one picture per idea, no decoration; one loud thing at a time
mayer.signalling: visual_change fields name what changes on screen
mayer.redundancy: narration carries the story, on-screen text kept to a few words
mayer.contiguity: labels sit on the faded icon, timelines and gap list
mayer.segmenting: five sections, each with one idea
mayer.pre_training: sec1 names fading before sec3 and sec4 use it

arcs.attention: cartoon colleague in a recognisable stuck moment
arcs.relevance: the viewer's own training and the Monday step
arcs.confidence: ten-minute steps, misses framed as expected
arcs.satisfaction: Sam's task resolved and the viewer picks their own
